facts.value: An evergreen shrub or small tree in the heath family (Ericaceae).
Native to the Mediterranean Basin and Western Europe.
The rough-surfaced, spherical fruit ripens red and matures in about 12 months, in autumn at the same time as the next flowering.
Fruit-eating birds often disperse the seeds.
It is grown as an ornamental tree or shrub, and its hard wood is used for firewood and pipes.
qualifiers: The wood is generally unsuitable for construction because the tree does not usually grow straight.

details.use: Eaten fresh; the fruit is sweet when reddish.
Used for jam, marmalades, yogurt, and alcoholic drinks, including Portuguese medronho and Albanian raki kocimarje.
details.scope: Portugal and regions of Albania for the named drinks; other uses are not geographically scoped in the source.

summary: The strawberry tree is an evergreen shrub or small tree native to the Mediterranean Basin and Western Europe. Its rough red fruits take about a year to mature, so autumn can bring ripe fruit alongside the next flowers, while birds help disperse the seeds. The fruit is eaten fresh when ripe and also made into preserves, yogurt, and regional spirits. The plant is also valued ornamentally and for its hard wood.

facts.value: A medium-sized evergreen oak tree.
Native to southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa.
Its thick bark is the primary source of cork for bottle stoppers, flooring, insulation, sports equipment, and other products.
qualifiers: The first harvest usually occurs after about 25 years; subsequent harvests are generally spaced nine to twelve years apart and can be repeated without greatly damaging the tree.

facts.value: Its insulating cork bark allows the tree to survive fire and regrow branches into the canopy.
Cork oak woodlands support many animal and plant species.
qualifiers: The source links declining demand for bottle corks with risks to these cultural landscapes and their biodiversity.

facts.value: The acorns are used as livestock feed in extensive pig fattening, including Iberian ham production.
qualifiers: Holm oak is preferred because its acorns are sweeter.

summary: Cork oak is a medium-sized evergreen tree native to southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa. Its thick, insulating bark helps it survive Mediterranean fires and is harvested repeatedly for cork once trees mature, supplying products from bottle stoppers to flooring and insulation. The woodlands also support rich plant and animal communities, while their acorns are used to feed pigs in extensive farming systems.

facts.value: A creeping, mat-forming succulent.
Native to South Africa.
Grows on coastal and inland slopes and often acts as a pioneer on disturbed sites.
facts.scope: South Africa, from Namaqualand through the Western Cape to the Eastern Cape

facts.value: Produces yellow flowers from April to October; they open in bright morning sunlight and close at night.
Its flowers attract several kinds of bees and beetles, its leaves, flowers, and fruits feed various animals, and its dense clumps shelter small animals.
Naturalised widely and invasive in several regions, where it can form extensive single-species stands, reduce biodiversity, and compete with threatened plants.
facts.scope: Especially Australia, California, and the Mediterranean

details.use: Eaten fresh or made into a very tart jam.

summary: Sea fig is a creeping, mat-forming succulent native to South Africa, where it grows on coastal and inland slopes and often colonizes disturbed ground. Its yellow flowers open in bright morning light and support bees and beetles, while several animals eat its foliage, flowers, or fruit. The ripe fruit is eaten fresh or made into tart jam. Beyond its native range, dense invasive mats can displace other vegetation.
reviewFlags: The food-use claims in s1:p23 are marked citation needed in the source.

facts.value: A yellow-flowering member of the wood-sorrel family whose tissues have a sour taste associated with oxalic acid.
Indigenous to South Africa.
Produces many small underground bulbs and, across much of its non-native range, reproduces largely vegetatively.
facts.scope: Non-native range for predominantly vegetative reproduction
qualifiers: Many non-native populations have only one style length and do not produce seed.

facts.value: An invasive species and noxious weed in many regions outside South Africa.
facts.scope: Including coastal California, Europe, the Middle East, and Australia

facts.value: The plant has been used as a source of oxalic acid, food, folk medicine, and yellow dye.
qualifiers: Medicinal use is historical or traditional and does not establish efficacy.

details.use: Used as food in some parts of the world.
details.conditions: The source says boiling can reduce risks associated with high calcium oxalate levels.
Modest quantities are described as reasonably harmless to humans and livestock.

details.use: Eaten raw or boiled and served with milk.
details.conditions: Raw or boiled, according to the source.

details.effect: Oxalic acid is reported as toxic in large quantities.
details.conditions: Large quantities; boiling plant parts is reported to reduce risk.

details.effect: Heavy consumption can cause chronic oxalate poisoning, tetany, renal damage, or death.
details.conditions: Gorging on dense growth or consuming large quantities, especially when hungry; reports include South Australian pastures.
details.scope: Outside South Africa, including South Australia

summary: Bermuda buttercup is a sour-tasting, yellow-flowered wood sorrel indigenous to South Africa. It produces abundant underground bulbs, a trait that helps it spread vegetatively and makes it a persistent invasive weed in several other regions. Although parts of the plant have documented culinary uses, they contain oxalic acid: the source reports risks from large quantities and describes serious or fatal poisoning when livestock gorge on dense growth.
reviewFlags: The human hazard discussion in s1:p15 appears in a section marked original research and includes citation-needed warnings; its claims require further review.

facts.value: A perennial herbaceous orchid.
Its flower has three large purple sepals and a hairy, patterned labellum that resembles a bee's abdomen.
Usually grows in semi-dry turf, grassland, calcareous dunes, limestone sites, or open woodland, including disturbed places such as old quarries, verges, and airfields.
qualifiers: Prefers well-drained, nutrient-poor calcareous soils in bright or dim light.

facts.value: Northern populations are almost exclusively self-pollinating, while in the Mediterranean male long-horned bees may attempt to mate with flowers that mimic female bees in scent and appearance, transferring pollen in the process.
Depends on symbiotic mycorrhizal fungi, especially during germination, which may take months or years underground.
qualifiers: The source identifies Tulasnella and possibly other fungal genera.

facts.value: Reported as protected in Northern Ireland, Endangered in Turkey, Ukraine, and the Carpathian Mountains, and Critically Endangered in the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

details.use: Ground into salep, historically in the Ottoman Empire and still used in traditional dishes in Turkey and elsewhere in the Middle East.
details.scope: Historically the Ottoman Empire; currently Turkey and the Middle East

summary: The bee orchid is a perennial herb whose hairy, patterned lower petal resembles a bee. Northern populations mostly self-pollinate, but in the Mediterranean the flowers can lure male long-horned bees with visual and scent mimicry, allowing pollen transfer during attempted mating. It also depends on mycorrhizal fungi, particularly for its slow underground germination. Its tubers have historically been ground into salep for traditional foods and medicines.

facts.value: A flowering plant in the family Plumbaginaceae.
Endemic to the southwestern Iberian Peninsula.
Known from a single Portuguese locality in meadows on somewhat moist sandy soils.
qualifiers: This describes knowledge reported in the 2020 Portuguese Red List source.

facts.value: Assessed as Critically Endangered after continuing national declines exceeding 80% over recent decades; only one known population nucleus containing one adult individual remained.
qualifiers: Red List published in 2020 from assessments conducted in 2016–2019.
Reported pressures include changes to soil hydromorphism at the sole known site.

facts.value: Not protected under Portuguese or European Community legislation according to the supplied source.
qualifiers: The source provides no date for this legal-status statement.

summary: Armeria gaditana is a flowering plant endemic to the southwestern Iberian Peninsula. In mainland Portugal, the 2020 Red List knew it from just one meadow site on somewhat moist sandy soil in the eastern Algarve. Following a decline of more than 80% over recent decades, the national population was assessed as Critically Endangered, with only one known adult and continuing pressure from altered soil-water conditions.
reviewFlags: The legal-protection statement in s1:p7 has no date and should be checked before use.

facts.value: A conifer tree in the family Araucariaceae.
Endemic to New Caledonia in Melanesia.
A narrowly conical tree with a slender, spire-like crown, reaching up to 60 metres in its native habitat; its bark peels in rough, grey, resinous, paper-like sheets or strips.
facts.scope: Native habitat for maximum reported height

facts.value: A 2017 study found that trees tend to grow upright at the Equator, lean south in the Northern Hemisphere, and lean north in the Southern Hemisphere.
facts.scope: Cultivated or occurring trees across hemispheres

facts.value: Cultivated as an ornamental tree in warm regions around the world.
facts.scope: Locations listed include parts of Australia and New Zealand, Southern California, Puerto Rico, Mexico, India, the Philippines, Hawaii, Brazil, Singapore, and Southeast Asia.
qualifiers: It has sometimes been confused in cultivation with Norfolk Island pine.

summary: Cook pine is a tall, narrowly conical conifer endemic to New Caledonia, with a slender spire-like crown and bark that peels in paper-like strips. A 2017 study found a striking geographical pattern in its posture: trees tend to lean toward the Equator, while those at the Equator grow upright. Widely planted as an ornamental in warm regions, it has often been confused in cultivation with Norfolk Island pine.

facts.value: A shrub in the nightshade family (Solanaceae).
Native to South America.
Naturalised in North America, Europe, Australia, and New Zealand.
facts.scope: North America, Europe, Australia, and New Zealand

summary: Tall nightshade is a shrub in the nightshade family, native to South America. It has become naturalised well beyond that range, including in North America, Europe, Australia, and New Zealand.

reviewFlags: The supplied article is primarily about Ranunculus polyanthemos and treats Ranunculus tuberosus only as a synonym of R. polyanthemos subsp. nemorosus; taxon identity and claim scope require review before species-level facts are used.
